title: Bangladesh’s gender pay gap is reinforced by labor-market sorting, unpaid care, informality, and weak enforcement
source_unit: ILO, The gender pay gap in Bangladesh: Trends, causes and policy options
geography: Bangladesh, using the 2023 Labour Force Survey with stakeholder consultations and policy analysis

observations.period: Bangladesh labor market; 2023 employment and wage-employment structure

denominator.unit: national labor-market frame from the 2023 Labour Force Survey

employment_rate.value: female employment is 40.2% compared with 77.9% for men, a 37.7 percentage-point employment-rate gap

wage_employment_access.value: 19% of employed women are wage employees compared with 48% of employed men
wage_employment_access.unit: percent of employed women and men

representation.value: women represent about 17% of all wage employees and 6.2% of managerial positions

sorting_mechanism.value: gender inequality is produced before pay comparison through unequal access to wage employment, managerial work, and higher-paid sectors and occupations

observations.method: Descriptive analysis of Bangladesh’s 2023 Labour Force Survey, disaggregated by sex, employment status, sector, occupation, age, education, rurality, and formality, supplemented by stakeholder consultations.
observations.uncertainty: The national survey describes labor-market structure but does not identify a single causal source for each employment gap or establish how much of the gap would disappear under a specific policy.
observations.subgroup: Women and men in Bangladesh, wage employees, own-account workers, managers, informal workers, rural and urban workers, employers, and caregivers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Employment-status differences can reflect constrained opportunities, preferences, household production, or measurement and classification choices; the descriptive figures alone cannot distinguish these mechanisms.

observations.period: Bangladesh wage employment; monthly wage comparisons in 2023

denominator.unit: wage-employed women and men observed in the 2023 Labour Force Survey wage comparison

monthly_gender_pay_gap.value: women’s monthly earnings are approximately 22-25% lower than men’s, or about 750-780 taka for every 1,000 taka earned by men

age_pattern.value: the gap widens sharply with age, consistent with accumulating constraints after childbirth and across career progression

education_pattern.value: the gap narrows with higher education but does not disappear

formality_pattern.value: the gap is substantially higher among informal workers than among formal workers

observations.method: Monthly wage comparisons and distributional analysis using the 2023 Labour Force Survey, including age, education, and formal/informal employment breakdowns.
observations.uncertainty: The report’s monthly wage gap is not a randomized or longitudinal estimate; observed age, education, and formality gradients may combine selection, sector composition, experience, discrimination, hours, and other unobserved factors.
observations.subgroup: Women and men in formal and informal wage employment, younger and older workers, workers with different education levels, and workers entering or remaining after childbirth.
observations.counterinterpretation: Education and formal legal coverage may reduce disparities without proving that either factor is sufficient; monthly wages also differ from hourly pay and total household income.

observations.period: Bangladesh wage distribution and household-care context; 2023 survey and consultation evidence

denominator.unit: decomposition and household-care evidence across the reported wage distribution

unexplained_share.value: at all points of the wage distribution, the majority of the pay gap is not attributed to observed differences in education, occupation, or sector
unexplained_share.unit: majority share of gap; exact share varies by specification

care_time.value: women in wage employment report almost four times more weekly hours on household chores than men

sector_valuation.value: sectors with a relatively high share of female wage employment tend to offer lower average wages for all workers

institutional_route.value: equal-pay law, wage-setting, labor inspection, complaint access, care policy, and social dialogue are the proposed levers for converting formal rights into realized wage equality

observations.method: Wage-gap decomposition across the wage distribution, household-chore evidence from the survey, sector wage comparisons, qualitative stakeholder consultation, and review of Bangladesh’s legal and policy framework.
observations.uncertainty: An unexplained decomposition component is not itself proof of direct discrimination; the report combines quantitative associations and qualitative evidence, and does not estimate the causal effect of inspection, care policy, bargaining, or complaint mechanisms.
observations.subgroup: Women with unpaid-care responsibilities, workers in feminized sectors, informal workers, labor inspectors, employers, unions, policymakers, and workers using complaint or bargaining channels.
observations.counterinterpretation: Sector wage differences may reflect productivity, job amenities, hours, risk, or selection as well as undervaluation; care responsibilities and labor-market choices may be jointly determined by wages, norms, and available services.

related_sources.claim: Official ILO publication page, date, study scope, headline 22-25% monthly gap, methodology, consultations, and policy framing.
ILO publication DOI and bibliographic identifier.

boundary: This record adds a national labor-market and institutional-enforcement layer to the child-penalty finding. It is descriptive and decomposition-based evidence from Bangladesh’s 2023 survey, not causal proof that discrimination, unpaid care, informality, or a specific legal weakness independently causes the measured gap; it does not establish household welfare, lifetime earnings, or universal cross-country magnitudes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO PDF, publication page, 2023 Labour Force Survey basis, employment and wage-employment structure, 22-25% monthly gap, age, education, formality, decomposition, household chores, sector valuation, managerial representation, legal framework, stakeholder consultations, and policy boundaries were reviewed.
